title: ExportersIndia loses appeal: why online trade platforms must check what sellers list
subtitle: The consumer commission upheld a Rs 20 lakh penalty over explosive chemical listings and said an online marketplace cannot hide behind the safe harbour rule.
content_html:
Picture an online trade market where anyone with a phone number and an email address can sign up and ask sellers for prices. Now picture explosive chemicals sitting on that market like ordinary goods, with a friendly button that says "Get Best Quotes". That is what India's consumer watchdog found on ExportersIndia.com. On Monday, 16 November 2026, the consumer affairs ministry said the national consumer commission had dismissed the appeals of Weblink.In Private Limited, the company behind ExportersIndia, in orders dated 12 November. A Rs 20 lakh penalty now stays in place.

The bigger lesson is not about one company. It is about every online market where Indian traders and exporters meet buyers. The ministry said such markets cannot lean on their middleman status when the goods are dangerous and need a licence.

First, what is a B2B marketplace?

B2B means business to business. A chai stall that sells a cup to a student is selling straight to a person. A seller in B2B trade sells to other businesses, the way a dairy sells milk in bulk to that chai stall.

A B2B marketplace is an online version of a big wholesale market. Sellers put up their products. Buyers, usually other businesses, send an enquiry and ask for a price. The marketplace does not usually own the goods. It connects the two sides, a bit like a matchmaker for traders.

Take ExportersIndia, one such market. A review by the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA), India's consumer watchdog, also looked at IndiaMART, Justdial, Dial4Trade, Sigma-Aldrich India, Ibuychemikals and TradeIndia, according to Business Today.

What exactly went wrong?

The CCPA issued two final orders. The first, dated September 8, was about ammonium nitrate and PETN (pentaerythritol tetranitrate). The second, dated September 10, was about picric acid. Each order carried a penalty of Rs 10 lakh, so the total came to Rs 20 lakh, Business Standard reported.

A penalty is a fine for breaking a rule. Here, the CCPA called the listings a misleading advertisement and an unfair trade practice. A misleading advertisement is an ad that hides or twists an important fact. An unfair trade practice is a dishonest way of selling.

The important facts that were missing, as per the ministry, were simple:

  • The listings did not say these chemicals are notified explosives under Indian law.
  • They did not say a licence is needed to buy or sell them.
  • They did not warn that holding them without permission is punishable.
  • Sellers carried a "verified" tick, though the company admitted it did not check the licence of any seller or buyer.

The CCPA also listed gaps in the checks. Sellers' licences from the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO) were not shown. Buyers were not checked. There were no tracking safeguards required by the Ammonium Nitrate Rules, 2012. And there were no warnings about legal limits on use.

What is "safe harbour", and why did it not work here?

Think of a notice board outside a college canteen. If a student pins up a rude note, nobody blames the canteen owner. The owner only runs the board. That idea, in law, is called safe harbour.

In India, safe harbour comes from Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the main law on electronic commerce, in force since 17 October 2000. It protects an intermediary, which means a middleman platform that only carries content put up by others, from being blamed for that content.

But the protection comes with a condition. The platform must follow due diligence. Due diligence means taking reasonable care, like a school guard checking a visitor's ID card at the gate instead of letting everyone walk in.

Weblink.In argued it was only an intermediary under Section 79, had no actual knowledge of the listings, and that no specific law asked it to verify the licences of sellers and buyers, Business Today reported. The CCPA rejected this, holding that intermediary protection depends on following due diligence rules. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), the national consumer commission, agreed. It also held that removing listings only after they were caught was not enough.

The company had also called itself just a B2B directory. That claim was not accepted either, because anyone could register with a phone number and an email address and ask for any amount, the ministry said, as reported by Business Standard.

This video discusses safe harbour under Section 79 in simple terms, for readers who want the legal idea in more detail.

One fine, or a wider sweep?

It is a wider sweep. In October, the ministry said the CCPA's action had led to the delisting of 3,940 sellers and listing entries across these platforms, Inc42 reported. IndiaMART had the most, with 3,092. ExportersIndia had 421, Justdial 206 and TradeIndia 166.

Other cases are moving too:

  • Dial4Trade Technologies was fined Rs 10 lakh over ammonium nitrate listings, and the NCDRC dismissed its appeal on 9 October 2026.
  • Justdial got a Rs 10 lakh penalty in an order dated 28 October, and said the money was the only financial impact, according to Inc42.
  • Proceedings against IndiaMART, Sigma-Aldrich Chemicals, TradeIndia and Ibuychemikals are still under investigation, as per the CCPA.

The Hindi video below covers the earlier Rs 10 lakh fine on Dial4Trade, a case from the same review.

What does this change for exporters and online sellers?

For the platforms, the message from the ministry is direct. The NCDRC orders, it said, "reaffirm that platforms which host or promote listings of regulated and hazardous goods must exercise due diligence before listing such products and cannot rely on intermediary status to avoid responsibility under consumer protection law" (Business Standard).

For sellers, especially small traders and exporters who use these markets to find buyers, a few things follow from the sources:

  • The CCPA has run a sector-wide review of e-commerce platforms for listings of hazardous chemicals and explosives, so this is not a one-off check.
  • The CCPA expects platforms to make sure sellers display valid licences issued by the explosives safety body, Inc42 reported.
  • A "verified" badge has to mean something. Showing a tick without checking was one of the reasons for the penalty.

For ordinary people, there is a simple tool. Anyone can report listings of explosives on online platforms through the national consumer helpline at 1915, the ministry said.

The short version

An online market is like the owner of a big wholesale mandi. Nobody expects the owner to taste every mango. But if someone is openly selling something dangerous at stall number five, with a "verified" sticker from the owner, the owner cannot say it was not their business. That, in plain words, is what the 12 November orders say.
